common_name: Alba Plena Wood Anemone (Old Double White-Flowered Selection)

planting.note: Plant thin, brittle rhizomes 2 inches deep in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Alba Plena is one of the oldest recorded double-flowered wood anemone selections, known in cultivation since the 1500s.

directions: Plant the thin rhizomes shallowly in fall in cool, humus-rich woodland soil beneath deciduous trees where spring light is plentiful but summer shade is deep. Alba Plena carries a loosely doubled ruff of narrow white petals surrounding a small green-tinted center, a subtler and more antique-looking double than the fuller pompon of 'Vestal', opening in early to mid spring. Like the species it goes fully dormant by early summer, so pair it with later-emerging ferns or hostas, and avoid disturbing established colonies since the rhizomes spread and increase slowly on their own.

common_name: Leeds Variety Wood Anemone (Large Pale Lavender-Blue Selection)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Leeds Variety is an Award of Garden Merit selection prized for flowers noticeably larger than the wild species.

directions: Set the brittle rhizomes shallowly and horizontally in fall into cool, moisture-retentive woodland soil beneath deciduous trees or shrubs. Leeds Variety produces unusually large, rounded, pale lavender-blue flowers held on sturdy stems above ferny, deeply cut foliage in early to mid spring, a vigorous and long-cherished selection that reliably outperforms the species in flower size. It goes fully dormant by early summer and spreads gradually by creeping rhizome into an increasing carpet, best left undisturbed once sited in a permanent shaded location.

common_name: Ingramii Grecian Windflower (Vigorous Deep Blue-Violet Selection)

planting.note: Plant tubers in fall, after soaking briefly to rehydrate, in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Ingramii is a vigorous, larger-flowered selection in deep blue-violet, considered one of the finest color forms of the species.

directions: Soak the small knobby tubers before planting, then set them 2 inches deep in fall in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun beneath deciduous trees. Ingramii bears exceptionally deep blue-violet, daisy-like flowers larger than the typical species and holds an Award of Garden Merit for its vigor and rich color, opening in early to mid spring and closing at night and in overcast weather. It naturalizes readily by tuberous rhizome to form an expanding carpet before going summer-dormant, and combines beautifully with pale or white spring bulbs for contrast. Once established it needs no routine care and resents disturbance, so choose a permanent site.

common_name: Charmer Grecian Windflower (Deep Rose-Pink Anemone Blanda)

planting.note: Plant tubers in fall, after soaking briefly to rehydrate, in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Charmer bears deep rose-pink flowers, a richer pink than most other named Anemone blanda forms.

directions: Rehydrate the dried tubers by soaking briefly, then plant 2 inches deep in fall in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun under deciduous trees or shrubs. Charmer produces saturated rose-pink, daisy-like flowers with a pale central boss of stamens, deeper and warmer in tone than the softer pinks of many other blanda selections, opening in early to mid spring and closing at night and in cloudy weather. It spreads gradually by tuberous rhizome to form an increasing carpet beneath deciduous canopy before going dormant by early summer, and pairs well with blue or white anemone blanda cultivars for a mixed spring tapestry. Once established it requires no routine care and resents disturbance, so choose a permanent planting site.

planting.note: Plant divisions or nursery starts in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; kidney saxifrage forms a low evergreen mat and tolerates deeper shade than most other mossy saxifrages.

directions: Plant divisions in spring in cool, humus-rich, evenly moist soil in partial to full shade, where its rounded, softly hairy, kidney-shaped evergreen leaves form a dense, slow-spreading mat. In late spring to early summer, wiry, gently branched stems rise well above the foliage carrying loose, airy sprays of small white flowers, each petal flecked with tiny yellow and red spots. Native to shaded rock crevices and woodland banks in the Pyrenees and a few relict Irish sites, it is one of the more shade-tolerant members of its group and works well tucked among rocks, at the front of a woodland border, or edging a shaded path. Keep soil consistently moist but well drained, since it dislikes both drought and standing water.

common_name: Blackberry and Apple Pie Fortune's Saxifrage (Deep Maroon-Leaved Fall Bloomer)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade sheltered from harsh winter wet and wind; this cultivar's deep maroon foliage color is richest in bright shade.

directions: Plant divisions in spring into consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, sheltered from drying wind and winter waterlogging. Blackberry and Apple Pie forms a low mound of rounded, scalloped leaves in deep maroon-purple with even darker undersides, among the darkest foliage color found in the fortunei group, which lights up a shaded corner through summer and fall. In September and October it sends up airy, branched sprays of small white to pale pink flowers with distinctly elongated lower petals, giving each bloom an asymmetrical, wispy look that is one of the last floral displays of the shade garden season. Give it steady moisture and good drainage, and mulch lightly in cold climates since it is somewhat less hardy than the plain species.

planting.note: Transplant rooted divisions in early spring into cool, acidic, humus-rich soil with sharp drainage in deep to partial shade, ideally on a shaded slope where water never stands.

directions: Transplant rooted divisions in early spring into cool, acidic, humus-rich soil with excellent drainage in partial to full shade. Nippon bells forms a slowly creeping mat of glossy, rounded, leathery evergreen leaves that bronze attractively through winter, and in early spring each wiry stem lifts a single large, nodding, fringed bell-shaped flower in pink or white, larger and borne singly compared to the clustered blooms of its relative Shortia soldanelloides. This Japanese mountain woodland native performs best where summers stay cool and moist and resists heavy clay or soil that dries out; it is a choice subject for a shaded rock garden or peat bed alongside other ericaceous woodland plants.
